sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Pro-Changers (Swarajists)**: Led by **C.R. Das** and **Motilal Nehru**, they advocated for 'entering the councils' to obstruct British policy from within.
• **No-Changers**: Led by **Vallabhbhai Patel**, **Rajendra Prasad**, and **C. Rajagopalachari**, they emphasized 'constructive work' (Khadi, untouchability, national education) and Gandhian non-cooperation.
• **Emergence of Left Wing**: **Jawaharlal Nehru** and **Subhash Chandra Bose** emerged as the voice of the youth, demanding 'Purna Swaraj' and linking the national struggle with global anti-imperialism.
• **Key Metric**: The 1923 Swarajist electoral victory in the Central Legislative Assembly forced the British to appoint the **Muddiman Committee** to review the 1919 Act.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix
rows: C.R. Das (President), Motilal Nehru (Secretary). Base: Bengal, Central Provinces.
Obstructionism from within the legislature to expose the 'sham' of the 1919 Act.
Prelims: Focus on the Swaraj Party formation (1923) and their legislative tactics.
Patel, Prasad, Rajagopalachari. Base: Rural India, Ashram networks.
Focus on grassroots mobilization and social reform to prepare for future mass movements.
Mains: Role of constructive work in building the 'social base' of the Congress.
Nehru, Bose. Base: Pan-India, Student/Labor unions.
Demand for complete independence (Purna Swaraj) vs. Dominion Status.
Prelims: Independence for India League (1928) and Lahore Session (1929).

items.definition: Formed in 1923 after the Gaya Session of Congress; aimed to wreck the 1919 Reforms from within the Legislative Councils.
A Gandhian strategy involving spinning, prohibition, and removal of untouchability to build a disciplined, self-reliant nation.
Founded in 1928 by Nehru and Bose to pressure the Congress to adopt 'Complete Independence' as its goal.

items.title: Major Applications / Initiatives
items.content:
• **Legislative Obstruction**: Swarajists successfully defeated the government budget in 1924.
• **Social Reform**: No-Changers focused on the Vaikom Satyagraha (1924-25) to address caste-based discrimination.

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content:
• **Challenges**: Internal rift between Pro-Changers and No-Changers threatened Congress unity.
• **Solutions**: The 'Gandhi-Das Pact' (1924) allowed Swarajists to work on behalf of the Congress, maintaining organizational integrity.

items.title: Mnemonic for Retention
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym**: 'S-N-R' (Swarajists, No-Changers, Radicals).
• **Decoded Meaning**: S (Swarajists: C.R. Das/Motilal), N (No-Changers: Patel/Prasad), R (Radicals: Nehru/Bose).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often confuses the 'Swaraj Party' with the 'Swarajist faction' within Congress. Remember, they were part of the Congress, not a separate political party in the modern sense.
Mains Value Addition: Use the term 'Ideological Pluralism' to describe the 1920s Congress, showing how it accommodated both constitutionalists and radicals.

keyTakeaways: The 1920s was a period of 'political lull' that was actually a phase of intense internal consolidation.
The Swarajists provided a platform for political activity when mass movements were not feasible.
The rise of Nehru and Bose signaled the shift from moderate constitutionalism to radical anti-imperialism.
